items.content_html:
Reduces the number of dependencies for any user of services.qemuGuest by ~1715 requisites, including x265, SDL, ...etc. on headless systems.

More details (including how that number was calculated) can be found in each commit. Top level summary:

  • Add a pkg.qemu_ga target that builds the QEMU guest agent only as a minimal qemu build.- This makes it easier to reason with, apply overlays, or investigate the potential attack surface of this package.
  • Update the services.qemuGuest module to point to the new dedicated pkg
  • Added a release note that services.qemuGuest will no longer build documentation. That means anyone who uses services.qemuGuest will need to manually re-enable documentation afterwards or use the full qemu_kvm package like before.

  • Switched a Linux x86-64 qemu-kvm machine between the two module definitions, which happened without interruption

Fixes: #489197

Qemu is moving to a new way of doing UEFI var storage:
Context:

  • https://www.qemu.org/docs/master/devel/uefi-vars.html
  • https://gitlab.com/qemu-project/edk2/-/blob/master/OvmfPkg/QEMU_PV_VARS.md
  • https://gitlab.com/kraxel/virt-firmware-rs/-/blob/main/varstore/README.md?ref_type=heads

This attempts to do so, but the build hangs on aarch64-linux.

I suspect this is because of the edk2-var-generator usage inside the derivation:

  1. It shouldn't be necessary, if we move to the json var storage.
  2. It's... vastly overkill. virt-firmware has a python script that can do this, seemingly without running qemu...

So this is a draft, because there's more work/consideration that needs to happen, hopefully from EDK2/OVMF/qemu maintainers.

Using the target platform instead of the host allows us to build a targetted QEMU to the desired platform we want to test. For example, to test an ARM firmware, I can now call this to get a minimal QEMU:

pkgsCross.arm-embedded.buildPackages.qemu.override
{ targetCpuOnly = true }

Prior to this change, the QEMU would be built to execute x86-64 even if the specified target is ARM. This commit is the natural successor of the change I made to GDB [1].

items.content_html:
Summary

Adds virtualisation.bootDiskAdditionalSpace option to configure additional disk space beyond the NixOS closure when useBootLoader = true.

Problem

When virtualisation.useBootLoader = true, qemu-vm.nix creates a systemImage via make-disk-image.nix with additionalSpace = "0M" hardcoded. This means the backing disk image is sized exactly to fit the NixOS closure with zero free space.

Consequence: Any runtime writes fail with ENOSPC (no space left on device):

  • NixOS integration tests that write runtime data
  • Container runtimes pulling images (Docker, Podman)
  • Databases writing journals or data files
  • Applications creating logs or temporary files

The existing virtualisation.diskSize only controls the qcow2 overlay size, not the backing systemImage. This distinction is subtle and undocumented, leading users to expect diskSize to control total available space.

Related Context

The pattern of needing configurable disk space is well-established:

  • VirtualBox module exposes virtualisation.virtualbox.guest.baseImageFreeSpace for the same purpose
  • make-disk-image.nix defaults to additionalSpace = "512M", suggesting this headroom is expected—qemu-vm.nix overriding to "0M" appears unintentional

Changes

  • New option: virtualisation.bootDiskAdditionalSpace (type: string, default: "512M")
  • Wiring: Passes configured value to make-disk-image.nix additionalSpace parameter
  • Test: New qemu-vm-bootdisk-space test validating the option works

Test plan

  • Existing nixosTests.systemd-boot.basic passes
  • New nixosTests.qemu-vm-bootdisk-space passes (tests default 512M, custom 1G, minimal 64M configurations)

Notes for reviewers

Behavioral change: Default increases from "0M" to "512M" additional space. This matches make-disk-image.nix's own default and provides reasonable headroom. Users wanting the old behavior can set bootDiskAdditionalSpace = "0M".

Why a new option vs. respecting diskSize? The existing virtualisation.diskSize controls the qcow2 overlay size, not the backing systemImage. Overloading it would conflate two distinct concepts. A dedicated option is clearer and doesn't change overlay behavior.

items.content_html:
system.build.vm currently embeds startVM but does not expose it to the module system. This can make it considerably harder than necessary to customize system.build.vm with i.e. code to create and destroy additional resources on the host system, without vendoring all of startVM.

While introducing a custom system.build attribute might be a solution in some cases, much of the surrounding eco-system assumes VMs to be runnable via system.build.vm. Adhering to that convention allows one to run i.e. NixOS VM tests with a customized system.build.vm.

preVM/postVM attributes akin to pkgs.runInLinuxVM, etc were considered as an alternative, but would either provide suboptimal UX or require more code changes in a anready convoluted NixOS module.

This change should be a noop whenever one does not explicitly set system.build.vm to something other than the default. It supports the later by allowing e.g.:

 system.build.vm = lib.mkForce (
   hostPkgs.writeShellScriptBin "run-${config.system.name}-vm" ''
     ${createVmDisk}
     ${cfg.runner} $@
   ''
 );

items.content_html:
Description of changes

this renames qemu-vm.nix to qemu-guest.nix and changes it to function like other modules where it is imported unconditionally but with the options in it activated by setting a .enable = true; option.

This way vmVariant can be retired in favour of the more typical lib.mkIf (virtualisation.qemuGuest.enable), and qemu virtualisation options can be set unconditionally and only take effect when qemuGuest.enable = true;

This should be backward-compatible (modulo deprecation warnings) with the way things currently work. importing qemu-vm.nix will just set the .enable option, and vmVariant still works as it did before.

Reasoning

The current situation of needing to import qemu-vm.nix has the following disadvantages:

  • It works differently than any other module in nixos. This confused me when I first encountered it, and I've seen it confuse others. The error messages aren't great, because options (e.g. virtualisation.memorySize) just mysteriously aren't available.
  • Need extra machinery to make the options appear in the documentation.
  • Splits pure (flakes) from impure (non-flakes) nixos configurations because many configurations import <nixpkgs/nixos/modules/virtualisation/qemu-vm.nix> instead of using modulesPath.
  • vmVariant is also a different mechanism for conditional config inclusion than almost anything else in nixos. But it's doing essentially the same work as a normal mkIf.
  • if you want to use a configuration as a VM and also as not a VM, any config referring to virtualisation options has to be behind vmVariant. For most modules you can set those options unconditionally and then just toggle the .enable option.

Related issues:
#196755
#59219

I still need to add a release notes entry.

items.content_html:
Description of changes

VMs built with hardware.opengl.enable = true will now use opengl hardware acceleration backed by VirGL.

This makes it possible to run most Wayland compositors in a VM, and enables hardware acceleration for X11 desktop environments.

Hardware acceleration can also be enabled when running a test VM interactively with:

{
  interactive.nodes.machine = {
    virtualisation.opengl = true;
  };
}
nix run .#nixosTests.gnome.driverInteractive
>>> start_all()

Compositors like gamescope which rely on Vulkan still aren't supported out of the box. Although, it looks like we could eventually support this if we enable & use rutabaga when building qemu.

NOTE: I haven't tested this on aarch64-linux & darwin, but I assume it should work based on the similar usage instructions I found at https://github.com/knazarov/homebrew-qemu-virgl#usage---m1-macs.
